messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

When Meena Patel was assaulted, she was closing up the small discount store where she had worked for years. At 66, widowed and used to moving carefully through the routines of her shift, she had stayed late to straighten a back aisle and count returns. A man had lingered after the last customers, acting irritated about store policy, and when the front was nearly empty he cornered her in the stock area and raped her. What remained with her afterward was not a smooth story but a handful of brutally fixed images: the angle of the metal shelving against her shoulder, the look of his face when he realized no one else was nearby, the harsh stripe of light from the partially open door. She said remembering it was “like photographs,” as if certain moments came back already developed and staring at her, while the rest disappeared into blank spaces she could not fill in. A few scenes stood out with unbearable sharpness and between them there was nothing, only the knowledge that something terrible had happened.

In the months afterward, the world became full of moments that pulled those images back into her mind. The smell of smoke was especially powerful. If a customer came in carrying the odor of cigarettes on his jacket, or if there was even a faint burnt smell from overheated wiring or food from the neighboring shop, Meena would be yanked back to those frozen pictures before she could steady herself. Being alone with a man at work had the same effect. If she was stocking shelves and a male delivery driver remained in the aisle after others had gone, the scene in the stock room would flash up in fragments so vividly that the present moment seemed thin and unreliable. Even seeing people behave badly—someone shouting at a cashier, a man ignoring the rules of the line, a customer acting entitled and aggressive—could bring back the remembered snapshots of the assault, as though the violation in front of her and the violation done to her belonged to the same moral order.

Those same situations did more than trigger memory. They fed the meanings she had come to live by since the rape. When men lingered too close, or when she saw someone getting away with rude or bullying behavior, Meena felt again that what happened to her had been deeply unfair and that nothing had been set right. The ordinary sight of people misbehaving struck her with particular force; she would think that decency meant nothing, that people could harm others and carry on untouched. After a whiff of smoke or an unwanted moment alone with a man in the store, she often found herself thinking not only of the attack but of how much she had been reduced by it—that even a small upset now undid her, that she could no longer trust herself to cope with ordinary life. The day would flatten out after that. She had once taken pride in being reliable and composed; now she would go home feeling that nothing in her life held meaning in the same way anymore.

Over time those beliefs made the surroundings of her life feel increasingly dangerous. Meena had come to believe she could not handle “even the slightest upset,” and because of that she watched constantly for anything that might overwhelm her. At work she noticed every male customer who stayed in the store too long, every raised voice, every breach of manners. What frightened her most was not only the possibility of another assault but the certainty that if something even slightly threatening happened, she would fall apart. In that state, being alone with men felt charged before anything had actually occurred, and ordinary smells or minor confrontations stood out to her immediately as warnings. Her conviction that life no longer had meaning also narrowed her world; if little felt worth engaging in, the atmosphere of the store and the behavior of strangers seemed to matter only as possible signs of danger or injustice.

The memories themselves strengthened that vigilance. Because the assault returned as stark visual fragments rather than as something fully past, Meena responded to reminders as if the event were waiting to happen again. A smell of smoke did not stay just a smell; it summoned the stock room in pictures, and once those pictures came, she became even more alert to men nearby, to voices, to any trace of threat in the store. The blanks in her memory were troubling in their own way. She was unnerved by not knowing exactly what had happened in the missing stretches, and that uncertainty made her scan the present more sharply, as if she might prevent a repeat by catching danger earlier than before.

By the time she sought help, the pattern had tightened around her work and the rest of her life. She was still showing up for shifts, but she rearranged tasks to avoid being alone in the back with male coworkers or delivery staff, and tense interactions with customers could leave her shaken for hours. At home, she sat with the sense that the world had become morally broken and that her own strength had somehow drained out of her. What finally brought her in was a recent episode at the store: a man argued loudly over a return while another customer nearby smelled strongly of smoke, and the combination brought back the visual fragments so intensely that she had to step away from the register. She came to treatment frightened that this was now permanent—that a smell, a man, or one person’s bad behavior could keep taking her life from her—but still hoping that if she could understand why her mind kept returning to those moments, she might not have to live as if the assault were still happening.
